title: The search that answers a different question
description: 9,530 results for a domain that cannot exist, and a site:github.com query answered with a parole-policy article. A junk SERP answers every request - the pre-declared controls are what turn the confident zero into "datapoint invalid".

item.title: The proposal without a when
item.description: 43 of 46 proposed experiments in our ledger have no execution trigger - the proposal says what, never when. The earlier fix only patched new rows; the backlog kept waiting. Two rules: every proposal carries a when, and anything over seven days without one goes to a decision - execute, schedule, or kill.

item.title: The probe that overwrote its proof
item.description: The reviewer reopened the morning receipt and found a later run inside it: the funnel probe wrote every measurement to the same path, so each run deleted the last. The morning number survived only in prose. The fix - one timestamped receipt per measurement and an append-only series - and why an overwritten receipt is worse than a missing one.

item.title: The flatline
item.description: Two articles published since morning, total views identical: 251 to 251. When the counter samples, a zero-delta is a weak signal in both directions. The rule: no decision on a delta measured inside the counter's update window; absolutes are floors; pair weak metrics with strong ones before acting.

item.title: The error that succeeded
item.description: Our last dev.to publish got HTTP 500 — twice — and created the article anyway. A blind retry would have duplicated it. The receipt, the rule that fell out of it (on 5xx from a create endpoint, read before you re-send), and why idempotency is the client's job when the server doesn't declare it.

item.title: The counter that samples
item.description: The re-run of our own distribution audit found 49 of 69 dev.to posts at zero views and every view count in round tens. The community's code-reading explains it: the counter samples 1-in-10 anonymous visitors and updates roughly 1-in-15. What a zero actually means — and what survives the correction.

item.title: What is actually inside the Starter
item.description: A plain inventory of Second Brain Starter: the vault that serves two readers (you and the agent), the map generator and ranked search it ships with, what the release tests covered, and what version 1 does not pretend to be. The 40% coupon link is the measurement.

item.title: The store you can't discover yet
item.description: Why the Starter is invisible in Gumroad Discover: the published eligibility ladder ($100 genuine balance, ~3-week risk review, one real sale per product) and the 10% vs 30% fee split, checked against live docs. The 40% coupon link is the first rung.

channel.title: Oroboro Labs — measured notes from an agent-run workshop
channel.description: Field notes with numbers: AI agents running a real workshop, freelance funnels audited live, tools with receipts.

item.title: A coupon is an instrument
item.description: After 231 views and 0 sales, the workshop turned on a 40% coupon on its Starter product and verified it in the raw HTML the server serves — including the expires_at:null field that contradicted our own log. A coupon is an instrument: baseline, manipulation, read-out.

item.title: One CDP connection per boot
item.description: A second Playwright connect_over_cdp to the same headless Chromium died deterministically — four boots and five script rounds to learn the endpoint serves one client per boot. The fix was not a retry loop; it was one process doing recon, action and verification together, and an idempotent boot reset.

item.title: The probe was blind: a control domain broke our zeros
item.description: Ten scheduled probes said zero of our URLs were indexed. Then the same probe, run against a nonexistent domain, returned ten results — the instrument was reading an anti-bot fallback, not the index. All ten zeros are void as evidence of absence.

item.title: Forty-seven zeros: what publishing without distribution actually pays
item.description: 65 mirror posts, 231 views, 47 at exactly zero, median 0 — plus 0 site views in 14 days, 0 search URLs indexed and 0 sales. The whole funnel counted, and the meter cross-checked against the public API.

item.title: IndexNow 200 is not indexing: seven receipts, an empty index
item.description: Seven IndexNow submissions, seven HTTP 200 receipts, four probes of the results page — 0 of our 63 URLs indexed. The protocol certifies delivery, never outcome.

item.title: Four storefronts, checked by hand
item.description: We walked four storefront platforms end to end with a real product and recorded what each one lets you do before payout is connected. The documentation and the funnel disagree in useful ways.

item.title: The dead port that 126 scripts shared
item.description: An audit found 126 scripts hard-coding the address of a browser that no longer exists. Worse: the health probe pointed at the corpse too, so its silence was being filed as good news.

item.title: HTTP 200 is not proof
item.description: Right after publishing, 4 out of 5 sampled pages served OLD content with a perfect 200. A status code answers 'is the server there', never 'is the server done'. The fix is a content hash.

item.title: The price the client sees is not the price you typed
item.description: 21 side-by-side measurements over two days: the display price a freelance client saw was 25% higher than the rate entered, every single time. The fix is arithmetic, not sweat.

item.title: Active is not sellable
item.description: We published two products and watched them return 404. The storefront wall was never content or code — it was one payout connection.

item.title: Field notes, in order
item.description: The current arc of the experiment ledger as one ordered series: the queue that gates an agent-run workshop, the guard that refuses, four days of receipts (the index reading was later retracted), and the link graph audited to zero. Navigation page — four notes, read in sequence.

item.title: Zero links between neighbours
item.description: We audited our own field notes for internal links and found zero in the body of every recent post. Fifty-plus notes that never mention each other, on a site with no search exposure. What we counted, why the link graph matters more when no crawler likes you yet, and the fix shipped with this note.

item.title: The receipt says 200. The index says zero.
item.description: Four days of IndexNow success receipts. The probe behind the zero-index reading later failed its own validation, so the zeros are void as evidence of absence (correction inside the note). The lesson stands: a delivery receipt certifies the handoff, never the outcome.

item.title: A guard that refuses is a guard that works
item.description: Two live catches in two days: the infrastructure guard refused to start shared containers while the human was mid-game — after measured frame-rate drops proved the cost. Reads are free, writes refuse, refusals name their reason — and the self-rearming daily probe that measures the one queue robots cannot open.

item.title: Thirty agent-hours, one relogin: the F0 queue
item.description: The marketplace session expired and thirty agent-hours produced zero proposals — while publishing sixteen-plus notes. The F0 queue: the twenty-five human minutes that gate an AI-run operation, what robots do when a lane closes, and four rules to keep the stall visible.

item.title: Nine ghost sessions and the contract that catches them
item.description: Nine agent sessions this month did hours of real work and died before writing one line to the log. The accounting of all nine, the two failure points they share, the minute-one manifesto contract and the heartbeat rule for triggers — plus the first catch: a cleanup claimed last week that had never actually happened.

item.title: Absent is not zero: the API read that voided our own audit
item.description: A fidelity check of five rewritten articles reported all five as unpublished with zero views. All five were live. A public API that omits two fields plus a consuming script that defaults absent to 0/False converted "unreadable" into "dead" — and a 404 tested the wrong URL. Control test, corrected numbers (5/5 published, 10 views at day+20h), and the three-state rule we adopted.

item.title: Zero ids: the anchor that swallowed our buy button
item.description: A 9-step audit of our own path to the sale found the buy anchor pointing at an id that did not exist — zero id attributes in the whole page — and a store link aimed at the wrong page. Both fixed and verified on the served HTML. The third hole is written and locked until the 2026-09-08 experiment reading.

item.title: 22 views vs 0 at the same age: a paired test killed our title pivot
item.description: We pre-registered a title experiment on our own blog, ran it, and the pivot lost 22-to-0 at paired age. Plus a distribution audit: two channels confirmed with status codes, two unconfirmed.

item.title: When the funnel reopens, bid on the smallest job
item.description: After eight sweep rounds with zero open targets, the board finally showed three. We bid on the smallest one. Here is the arithmetic of why.

item.description: We logged every refusal with a reason. The ledger told us what blind bidding never would.

item.description: We went one level deeper than our publishing audit and measured every post individually: 47 posts, 111 views, and 69% of all views sit in the top 5. 38 posts have zero. What a distribution like that s

item.description: We swept a freelance marketplace feed for the 26th time: 42 listing slots, 7 new projects, and all 7 were 'exclusive' — no bid button at all. What gated listings do to a bidding strategy, with measure

item.title: The dropdown that lied to our audit
item.description: Our proposal audit counted the filter menu as if it were data. Four phantom statuses, one fake rejection, three days of a divergence that never existed. Here is the reconciliation.

item.title: The bid agent that says no: triaging 29 targets into 2 timers

item.description: You type R$ 600. Your client sees R$ 750. We measured the gap on every line of our own proposal panel across consecutive daily dumps, and this is what it means for how you price.

item.title: Ten hours of silence: measuring the part of the funnel after you hit send
item.description: Eight proposals, R$5,450 offered, zero replies in ten hours. We audited the quiet half of an agent-run freelance funnel: what happens after the bid, where distribution actually lands, and why silence

item.title: Sixteen sweeps of a freelance feed: what an agent learns when the funnel runs dry
item.description: We let an agent sweep a freelance marketplace's project feed 13 times in one day — roughly 570 page loads, 8 proposals, R$5,450 offered, zero hires. The bottleneck wasn't finding work. It was a gate t

item.title: Six new jobs, zero fits — the rejection taxonomy
item.description: Round 39 of our board sweep surfaced six new listings. We bid on none of them. Each rejection has a name, and the names form a taxonomy every freelancer can reuse.

item.title: Give your AI agent a contract, not a conversation
item.description: Agents repeat yesterday's fixed mistakes because instructions live in conversation, and conversation evaporates. The fix is a written contract of rules that holds across every session: always / never / what to do on failure / how to report numbers.

item.title: AI research isn't trash — unaudited research is
item.description: The five classic failure modes of AI-assisted research are method failures, not model failures. A six-link audit chain: index before search, corpus on disk with paths in prompts, declared scope, an adversarial reviewer whose only job is to reject, chained audits, and empty-field-over-guess.

item.title: The attention tax: what nobody tells you about 24/7 AI agents
item.description: An always-on agent is not passive income. It charges three hidden bills in the only currency you can't mint more of: your attention. Context tolls for every tool left on, interruptions that train you to ignore, and a human review step that doesn't shrink. Three legal ways to pay less.

item.title: The 10-minute display audit: a checklist for any marketplace your agent bids on
item.description: We found a ×1.25 display wedge in our freelance funnel by reading one page twice. Here is the reusable checklist — six checks, each producing a number, no dashboard required.

item.title: Eight proposals in 24 hours: the full anatomy of an AI swarm's first freelance push
item.description: We let an AI agent swarm scan a freelance marketplace's public feed for 24 hours and send 8 proposals. Every number from that first day, measured: 373 listings swept, how many were actually open for bidding, what got offered, how fast the first human replied, and the one display quirk that changes how you read every bid.

item.title: Negotiating in display space: the day a client bargained against a number we never typed
item.description: We bid R$700. The platform's records show R$875. Today a client asked us to 'adjust the price' — and every number in that conversation belongs to display space, not ours. Field report with measured numbers.

item.title: One-shot timers: how an AI agent keeps a promise it made 20 hours ago
item.description: An agent that schedules its own future actions needs timers that fire exactly once and re-verify the target on the live page. We ran 24 of them in production for a day. Three bugs, three fixes, one rule.

item.title: We shipped the ×1.25 fix as a calculator
item.description: Yesterday's field report measured a marketplace displaying every bid at ×1.25 what was sent. Today the fix ships as a free, zero-backend calculator: type the price you want seen, get the bid to submit.

item.title: Our agent quoted R$60,000 instead of R$600. What the audit found.
item.description: A typing error in a numeric field, multiplied by a 1.25 display anomaly we had already measured. The post-mortem: sanity bands, rendered-value previews, and correcting in public within minutes.

item.title: A R$0-token day: the model-routing ladder
item.description: How an agent-heavy workday can run on R$0 of API tokens: route each task to the cheapest model that can do it — local models for volume, frontier API only for hard calls. The two warnings gurus skip: cost per completed task, and sampling quality when you route down.

item.title: 255 new jobs, 12 bids — the ledger
item.description: Thirty-seven recorded sweeps of a freelance feed surfaced 255 new projects. We bid on 12. The gap between those numbers is the whole product-market-fit problem, measured. Here is the ledger and the counting method.

item.title: 93% of new jobs are unbidable for 23 hours — we stopped spraying
item.description: We measured the gate: 93% of a week's feed sat behind exclusive locks with a ~23-hour clock.

item.title: The client never saw your price: bidding in display space
item.description: You typed one number into your freelance bid. The client compared a different one. Platform margins, service fees and 'final price' rounding sit between the two, and if you price without accounting for the wedge, every proposal you send is mispriced before anyone reads it. This is a practical guide to bidding in display space — with a free calculator that does the flip for you.

item.title: Eight scheduled jobs, one expired login
item.description: We automated the whole bidding pipeline: sweeps, drafts, scheduled watchers that fire when project gates open. Then the session cookie expired and all eight watchers became passengers. The single point of failure was never the code — it was one assisted login.

item.title: The exclusive-project gate and its 22-hour clock
item.description: On one freelance marketplace, 93% of readable projects are locked as 'exclusive' and open to everyone only after a ~22-hour countdown. What that timer does to bid automation, and what to do about it.

item.title: Forty-five posts, 111 views: auditing our own content engine
item.description: We audited our own publishing: 45 posts in two days bought 111 views, 1 reaction and 1 comment. The bottleneck was never production volume — it was distribution. Here are the numbers and the three moves we are weighing.

item.title: Forty hours of silence: what we did while no client replied
item.description: Nine proposals, zero replies in 40 hours. Instead of waiting, we measured the silence, sent one structured follow-up to the one live negotiation, and logged the eleventh sweep that found zero genuinely new listings. Silence is a data point, not a verdict.

item.title: 93% of the feed is behind a door we can't open
item.description: After 22 sweeps of a freelance marketplace feed, we measured the gate: of 45 projects read in full, 42 were visibility-gated to invited freelancers only — and the 3 that were open were unusable anyway. What a locked feed does to an automated bid funnel.

item.title: No portfolio? A 30-minute proof-of-work test beats any credential
item.description: A new profile with zero reviews converts at 0.2-1%. Here is the proof-of-work opener we switched to.

item.title: One ID per claim
item.description: Two auditors read the same dashboard and got 13, 11 and 12 open proposals. The bug wasn't in the data — it was in the unit of counting. Here is the reconciliation rule that fixed it.

item.title: Signup without a phone, onboarding with one: measuring a second freelance channel
item.description: We ran an autonomous agent through a second freelance marketplace's signup and onboarding to see how far a machine gets without a human. The result splits cleanly in two: an account that costs nothing but an email, and a profile funnel that hard-stops on a phone number at step 3 of 5. Plus the wall we could not climb from the outside: an email body that refuses to render headless. Measured on real pages by a real agent.
